title: Jawi script
title_target: Rumi dan Jawi — dua wajah satu bahasa
goal: Read the Jawi on Malaysian signs, mosque names and banknotes — the Arabic script adapted for Malay, used for six hundred years before the Latin alphabet arrived.
bekal: recognizing the six extra letters that make Jawi different from the Arabic alphabet
reading short Malay words written in Jawi
knowing where Jawi is still used today and why it matters

notes: **Jawi** is the Arabic script adapted to write Malay. It has been used since around the 14th century, and for six hundred years **it was the only way Malay was written** — tales (*hikayat*), sultans' letters, religious books, laws and the first Malay newspapers were all in Jawi. The Latin alphabet (called **Rumi** in Malaysia) only replaced it in the 20th century under colonial rule.

**Rumi** is the Malaysian name for the Latin alphabet. *Tulisan Rumi* = Latin script. The word appears in all Malaysian language documents, including the name of the joint Indonesian–Malaysian spelling agreement (*Ejaan Rumi Bersama*).

**Mengaji** = to learn to read the Quran. Many Muslims learn this as children, so they **can already read the script** — what they haven't realized is that the same script can spell Malay words. A big head start that often goes unnoticed.
**Nampak** = to see, to be visible. *Tak pernah nampak* = have never seen. Very common in Malaysia, replacing *lihat* in many situations: *nampak tak?* = can you see it?

grammars.title: The six letters that make Jawi not Arabic
body: The Jawi alphabet uses all 28 Arabic letters and adds letters for Malay sounds that Arabic lacks. If you already read Arabic script, these are the only truly new ones.
after: Notice the pattern: **almost all of them add three dots** to the Arabic letter with the nearest sound. That's no accident — the designers picked the closest Arabic letter and marked it. Urdu, Persian and Ottoman Turkish scripts used the same trick for the same problem.

⚠️ The letter **ݢ** (ga) is the most distinctively Jawi — Persian and Urdu use a different shape for the same sound. If you see this letter, you're almost certainly looking at Malay, not Arabic, Persian or Urdu.

grammars.title: How Jawi spells vowels
body: This is the second big difference from Arabic, and it's exactly what makes Jawi **easier** to read than Arabic text without vowel marks.
after: Arabic writes short vowels with small marks (harakat) that are usually left out, so readers have to know the word already. **Jawi writes its vowels with full letters** — alif for *a*, ya for *i* and *e*, wau for *u* and *o*. So a Malay word in Jawi can be read even if you don't know it yet.

The only vowel usually **not** written is the weak **e** (ə, like the *a* in *about*) — that's why *beras* is written with just four letters (ب ر ا س becomes براس). It's also why beginners need to guess a little.

blocks.text: Malaysian signs use the same handful of words again and again. Learn their shapes — not spelling them out letter by letter, but recognizing the whole word, just as you recognize a familiar English word at a glance.
Look at **ڤجابت** (pejabat) and **ڤوليس** (polis) — both start with the three-dotted ڤ, the typically Jawi *p*. Once your eyes get used to that shape, signs start to become readable.

items: **Kelantan and Terengganu** — two states that require business signs to show Jawi alongside Rumi. This is where Jawi is most visible in daily life.
**Brunei** — Jawi has a strong position; government signs, department names and official publications use it widely.
**Banknotes and coins** — every ringgit note carries Jawi.
**Mosques and religious schools** — names, signs and publications.
**The Utusan Melayu newspaper** — a Malay-language paper in Jawi with a long history.
**Government department names** — many official Malaysian logos include the body's name in Jawi.
**Schools** — Jawi is taught in Islamic Education classes in Malaysian national schools.
**Patani, southern Thailand** — the Malay community there uses Jawi to write Patani Malay.

blocks.text: To be honest: Jawi's place is **a debated issue** in Malaysia. Some see it as Malay cultural heritage that should be revived; others, especially in non-Malay communities, question teaching it in schools. As a newcomer, the safest attitude is to appreciate it as historical heritage and stay out of the debate.

blocks.title: Why this unit is in an A1 module
items: **You may already know half of it.** If you've learned to read Arabic script (for example, for the Quran), you already know twenty-eight of the thirty-four letters.
**Signs are unavoidable.** If you go to Kelantan, Terengganu or Brunei, Jawi is on every street corner.
**It opens the door to history.** All classical Malay literature — *Hikayat Hang Tuah*, *Sejarah Melayu* (the Malay Annals), sultans' letters — is written in Jawi.
**It's not a requirement.** You can skip this unit entirely and still speak good Malay. It's a gift, not homework.

blocks.text: If you want to go further, Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka publishes a guide to standard Jawi spelling, and there are Jawi keyboards for phones and online Rumi–Jawi converters. Start by writing your own name — it's always the first word people learn, and always the one they remember best.
